items.title: 23.9 Hydrolysis of Acyl Chlorides, Alkyl Chlorides and Aryl Chlorides

source_refs.note: Topic 23.9 with Quick Check 23.5, answered (PDF 114-115); the equations are redrawn. The 14-day figure is the book's own; the Quick Check's peach and strawberry claim is not repeated. Exercises (PDF 115-117) are excluded. Answers need review.

blocks.text: The reactivity of acyl chlorides, alkyl chlorides and aryl chlorides can be compared by how easily they are hydrolysed:

items: Ethanoyl chloride reacts rapidly with water at room temperature: CH3COCl + H2O -> CH3COOH + HCl. Its carbonyl carbon carries a large partial positive charge, because two highly electronegative atoms, oxygen and chlorine, are attached directly to it, so water attacks it so fast that the reaction is complete within minutes.

Chloroethane is hydrolysed only on heating under reflux: CH3CH2Cl + H2O -> CH3CH2OH + HCl. Its carbon is attached to only one electronegative atom, chlorine, so it is less positive and water attacks it much more slowly; the reaction takes 14 days even at 100 C.

Chlorobenzene does not react with water. The carbon bonded to chlorine is part of the benzene ring, and a lone pair on chlorine is delocalised with the ring's pi electrons, giving the C-Cl bond some double-bond character; the bond is so strong that it does not break.

blocks.alt: Three reactions with water. Ethanoyl chloride, CH3-C(=O)-Cl, + H2O, 'Room temperature, rapid', gives ethanoic acid + HCl. Chloroethane, CH3-CH2-Cl, + H2O, 'Heat under reflux', gives ethanol + HCl. Chlorobenzene + H2O gives No Reaction.
